name: Unexpected Sign Extension
principle: A signed narrow integer is converted or promoted to a wider type and negative values are sign-extended with leading 1 bits. The resulting large or unexpected value becomes dangerous when used as a size, index, offset, delimiter, or application quantity.
detection_signals: assignment from signed char or short to int, long, size_t, unsigned int, or unsigned long
implicit integer promotion of signed char, short, or signed bit-field in arithmetic before assignment to wider type
bounds check on signed char or short followed by use as strncpy, memcpy, memmove, read, recv, malloc, new[], or array index
function length parameter receives signed char or short without range check after widening
cast or assignment chain signed short -> unsigned int or size_t where source can be negative
comparison like if (s > max) on signed narrow variable with no if (s < 0) check before unsigned use
bit-field value assigned to unsigned long on 64-bit target without explicit zero-extension cast
negative_signals: source type is unsigned char, unsigned short, uint8_t, uint16_t, or size_t and remains unsigned through the use
explicit range check rejects negative values before widening, e.g. if (s < 0 || s > max) error
value is widened to a signed type and validated after widening before any unsigned conversion
explicit zero-extension cast through matching unsigned narrow type, e.g. size_t n = (unsigned short)s, after validation
sink uses a constant bounded length independent of the widened value
false_defense_traps: checking only s > max on a signed short lets s == -1 pass and later become a huge unsigned length
casting to unsigned at the sink does not fix a negative value; it preserves the large converted value
testing only on 32-bit builds can miss 64-bit sign-extension behavior in long or pointer-sized arithmetic
assuming unsigned bit-fields always zero-extend can be wrong when integer promotion occurs first
null-terminating a destination buffer after strncpy does not prevent the oversized copy
verification_focus: Can a negative signed narrow value be widened or promoted and then used as a length, index, offset, delimiter, or quantity without rejecting the negative value?

consequence_chains.trigger: negative signed length is sign-extended and then interpreted as unsigned by a memory-copy API
consequence_chains.consequence: out-of-bounds read or write and possible memory corruption

consequence_chains.trigger: sign-extended value participates in size arithmetic that overflows before buffer access
consequence_chains.consequence: out-of-bounds read and information disclosure or crash

consequence_chains.trigger: range validation fails to reject negative narrow values before widening
consequence_chains.consequence: bypass of size or boundary checks

patch_principle: Use unsigned types for sizes, counts, indexes, and offsets that cannot be negative.
Reject negative values before any conversion to unsigned or pointer-sized types.
Validate again after widening when negative values are semantically allowed earlier.
Use explicit casts that document zero-extension only after range validation.
Compile with -Wconversion and -Wsign-conversion and review all reported narrow-to-wide conversions.

minimal_examples.vuln: short s = (short)0xFFFF; if (s <= 256) strncpy(path, input, s);
minimal_examples.safe: short s = (short)0xFFFF; if (s >= 0 && s <= 255) strncpy(path, input, (size_t)s);
